items.title: Nikkei study finds hidden debts of five US tech giants rise to $1.65 trillion due to opaque AI-related funding [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Five US tech giants' hidden debts soar to $1.65T on opaque AI funding
items.summary:
A Nikkei study reveals that hidden debts at five major US tech companies have surged to an estimated $1.65 trillion over four years, driven largely by investments in artificial intelligence. These off-balance-sheet liabilities, including data center leases and GPU supply contracts, now exceed the companies' reported debts, complicating risk assessment for investors.

The study highlights Meta's off-balance-sheet debt at about $420 billion, nearly triple its transparent debt, illustrating the scale of opaque financing in the AI sector. This rise in hidden liabilities reflects the growing capital demands of AI development and infrastructure, raising concerns about financial transparency among leading technology firms.

items.title: Report: China’s open-weight AI models gain global adoption as US export controls and proprietary strategies limit American AI ecosystem growth [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: China’s open-weights AI strategy is winning
items.summary:
China is advancing its AI strategy by openly releasing AI model weights, enabling broader adoption and innovation despite US export controls on GPUs and data sharing restrictions. This approach contrasts with American companies' proprietary models, which face limited ecosystem growth due to locked-down business practices and regulatory constraints. Chinese models are increasingly competitive, with companies like Moonshot and Alibaba claiming parity with leading US models at lower costs, contributing to widespread use in startups and various sectors across China.

The open-weight strategy allows Chinese enterprises to integrate AI models flexibly across manufacturing, research, and other industries, fostering a more effective global ecosystem than centralized, closed services. Meanwhile, US companies' focus on short-term profits and government export restrictions may hinder their long-term AI leadership and economic impact. Experts suggest that aligning incentives toward openness and public-interest AI technologies could be crucial for sustaining US competitiveness in the evolving AI landscape.

items.title: Stratechery analyzes Chinese AI models like Kimi K3 approaching state-of-the-art capabilities and their impact on AI economics and industry structure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Who's afraid of Chinese models?
items.summary:
Stratechery explores the implications of Chinese AI models such as Kimi K3 nearing state-of-the-art performance, focusing on how these models challenge assumptions about AI costs and industry dynamics. The analysis highlights the distinction between fixed research and development expenses and variable costs of running AI inference, emphasizing that open-weight models are not free to operate despite their availability.

The article discusses how token generation costs and model efficiency affect AI providers' economics, noting that tokens are not fungible commodities since different models require varying amounts of tokens to produce intelligence. This complexity influences the competitive landscape and the long-term structure of the AI industry, suggesting a shift back to fundamental economic principles in AI development and deployment.

items.title: Cursor experiments with agent swarms to build complex software tasks, improving efficiency and coordination with a new version control system [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Agent swarms and the new model economics
items.summary:
Cursor conducted experiments scaling agent swarms to cooperate on complex tasks, such as building a web browser and SQLite from scratch, demonstrating improved performance and stability over previous models. The system uses planner agents to decompose goals and worker agents to execute tasks, optimizing context management and coordination.

To handle the high volume of concurrent changes—up to 1,000 commits per second—Cursor developed a custom version control system that detects conflicts and supports coordination mechanisms beyond traditional human engineering practices. This approach aims to efficiently scale AI agent collaboration for diverse and complex software development challenges.

items.title: Study measures AI-generated writing in 12,750 arXiv papers, finds about one-third flagged as machine-written by 2026 with field-specific variation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How we measured AI writing across arXiv, and where the measurement breaks
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed the full text of 12,750 arXiv papers from 2021 to 2026 using a calibrated AI writing detector, finding that the share of papers flagged as machine-written rose from a 0.4% false-positive baseline pre-ChatGPT to about 32% by mid-2026, peaking near 39%. The study sampled ten academic fields monthly and used pre-ChatGPT papers as a control to set detection thresholds and account for false positives.

The flagged share varied widely by field, with computer science papers showing the highest AI writing prevalence at about 65%, while mathematics papers scored near 0.7%, though this low rate may reflect detector limitations rather than low AI use. The detector's sensitivity varies by model and writing style, and the results represent a lower bound on AI writing prevalence since some machine-generated text may evade detection. The study emphasizes that a flagged score indicates machine-like writing style but does not prove authorship or the extent of AI assistance.

items.title: Researchers propose Otap, a structure-aware optimal transport metric for evaluating agent trajectories by comparing execution graphs to valid solution graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Otap:Structure-Aware Optimal Transport for Evaluating Planning and Execution in Agent Trajectories
items.summary: Researchers introduce Otap (Optimal Transport for Agentic Planning), a new metric that evaluates large language model agent trajectories by measuring the distance between an agent's execution graph and valid solution graphs using an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport approach. Otap is designed to be invariant to dependency-preserving reorderings and robust to redundant or missing steps, addressing limitations of current binary success flags and exact matching metrics. The metric performs well on controlled perturbations and three public benchmarks, distinguishing valid from invalid trajectories even when semantics-only metrics fail, with highest accuracy when dependency graphs are precisely recovered.
items.description: Researchers introduce Otap (Optimal Transport for Agentic Planning), a new metric that evaluates large language model agent trajectories by measuring the distance between an agent's execution graph and valid solution graphs using an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport approach. Otap is designed to be invariant to dependency-preserving reorderings and robust to redundant or missing steps, addressing limitations of current binary success flags and exact matching metrics. The metric performs well on controlled perturbations and three public benchmarks, distinguishing valid from invalid trajectories even when semantics-only metrics fail, with highest accuracy when dependency graphs are precisely recovered.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.17082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks by generating trajectories that interleave planning, tool calls, and intermediate results. Current evaluation metrics reduce such a trajectory to a binary success flag or compare it against a reference by exact matching. A success flag cannot distinguish a sound solution from one that succeeds by luck, and says nothing about why a failed run went wrong. Exact matching penalizes plans that are valid but reordered or decomposed differently from the reference. We reframe trajectory evaluation as a distance between the agent's execution graph and a set of valid solution graphs, and instantiate it via an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport problem over attributed dependency graphs. The resulting score, termed \otap{} (Optimal Transport for Agentic Planning), is a pseudo-metric that is provably invariant to dependency-preserving reorderings and has bounded sensitivity to redundant steps. Its unbalanced marginals handle missing or hallucinated steps without forcing a match, and its soft coupling accommodates variation in plan granularity. On controlled perturbations and three public benchmarks, \otap{} separates valid from invalid trajectories in a regime where semantics-only metrics score below chance. Its accuracy is highest when the dependency graph is recovered exactly, and drops only when the graph is inferred heuristically from free-text traces.

items.title: WorldCupArena launches dynamic benchmark for language models and AI agents to predict 2026 FIFA World Cup matches with fine-grained evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: WorldCupArena: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Language Models and Deep-Research Agents on Football Forecasting
items.summary:
WorldCupArena introduces a dynamic benchmark designed to evaluate language models and deep-research agents on football match forecasting, starting with the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Models predict match results, scores, player events, statistics, and competition outcomes before kickoff, using either provided evidence or self-sourced information, with predictions compared against actual results after each match. The benchmark assesses result accuracy, exact-score accuracy, and a scoreline metric that credits near misses, covering 104 matches and 13 systems in its initial evaluation.

The benchmark allows continuous updates by adding new match schedules as they begin, enabling ongoing evaluation of future models without relying on known outcomes. Compared to betting-market and human-fan baselines, the top-performing system shows modest improvements in result and exact-score accuracy but clearer gains in the scoreline metric. The project’s code, prompts, predictions, and evaluation scripts are openly available on GitHub for community use and further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.18084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting a football match before kickoff requires more than knowing past results: a model must use changing information and make a clear prediction before the answer is available. We present WorldCupArena, a dynamic benchmark for language models and deep-research agents. The 2026 FIFA World Cup is its first evaluation, and the same process can be reused for future leagues and cups. Before each match, a model either receives a common evidence package or searches for information itself. It predicts the result and score, likely players and events, match statistics, and the outcome of the competition. After the match, these predictions are compared with the recorded result. New schedules can be added as they begin, allowing the benchmark to evaluate future models without using outcomes that are already known. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.16203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Document parsing is a foundational step for document understanding tasks such as visual question answering and key information extraction, as it transforms unstructured scanned images into structured representations by extracting textual, visual, and layout information. While numerous Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have been developed for this purpose, selecting an appropriate document parsing solution for a given document collection remains challenging, particularly in label-scarce settings. In this work, we conduct a systematic evaluation of text recognition performance across a diverse set of OCR engines and state-of-the-art MLLMs on multiple scanned document benchmarks spanning different domains and languages. Motivated by the limited contextual reasoning capabilities of many OCR engines and the high cost of manual annotations, we propose DocOCR-Eval, an annotation-free evaluation framework for automatic OCR assessment and selection. DocOCR-Eval employs a three-staged correction and ranking strategy to approximate annotation-based tool ordering without ground-truth labels. We show that aggregating across multiple MLLMs progressively improves alignment with annotation-based rankings. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that reliable OCR tool selection can be achieved in realistic, label-limited settings, providing practical guidance for deploying document parsing systems across diverse real-world document collections.

items.title: Researchers introduce 'weights to words' method to express and edit preference model inferences in natural language, improving interpretability and accuracy in diverse domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Weights to Words: Expressing and Editing Preference Model Inferences in Natural Language
items.summary:
Researchers present a method called 'weights to words' that converts high-dimensional preference model inferences into natural language descriptions paired with vector representations. This approach addresses challenges in understanding which factors drive decisions and allows users to inspect and edit preference models in real time. The method was demonstrated across domains including moral dilemmas, movies, wines, and large language model responses.

Two pre-registered human-subject experiments involving moral dilemmas and movie selection showed that regularizing preference models toward the learned natural language basis improved prediction accuracy on held-out data. Additionally, incorporating structured edits from participants further enhanced accuracy. Participants also preferred the inferred preference profiles and rated the method's predictions as more accurate compared to alternatives.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.16232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing use of statistical learning algorithms to infer human preferences from high-dimensional choice data runs up against a fundamental challenge: choice alternatives typically differ in many ways simultaneously, so it is generally unclear which factors actually drove an observed decision and should be credited as preferences. Compounding this problem, the opacity of these methods leaves human operators unable to inspect, contest, or correct models when they err. We introduce \emph{weights to words}, a method that takes a dataset of choice problems as input and automatically discovers a collection of domain-relevant preference dimensions, each described in natural language and paired with a vector in the model's representational space. These dimensions address both under-determination and opacity: they can be applied to concentrate attribution on a small set of meaningful factors, and they can externalize the model's inferences in natural language so that users can inspect and edit them in real time. We first qualitatively illustrate the method's versatility on four diverse domains: moral dilemmas, movies, wines, and free-form LLM responses. We then report two pre-registered human-subjects experiments, on moral dilemmas ($N=450$) and movie selection ($N=449$), that demonstrate its benefits for learning preference models: (1) regularizing a preference model toward the learned basis increases prediction accuracy on held-out choices, and (2) incorporating participants' structured edits further improves accuracy. In head-to-head comparisons, participants prefer the method's inferred preference profiles and endorse its predictions as more accurate.

items.title: Researchers propose CIGPO to improve multi-turn evidence-reading LLM agents by preventing reward-variance collapse in reinforcement learning, achieving 0.518 F1 on HotpotQA with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CIGPO: Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Evidence-Reading LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers identify instability in training multi-turn evidence-reading agents using outcome-only reinforcement learning, where intermediate turns receive little credit, causing optimization deadlock and format violations. They propose Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization (CIGPO), which assigns per-turn rewards based on the marginal increase in a reference model's log-likelihood of the correct answer to maintain reward variance and prevent collapse.

In experiments on HotpotQA with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, CIGPO improves the standard F1 score to 0.518 from a 0.252 baseline, outperforming the best GRPO checkpoint at 0.430 and avoiding the zero-advantage lock-in seen in GRPO. The approach uses separate normalization of information gain and F1 rewards along with a curriculum for weighting information gain, demonstrating that turn-level rewards can stabilize training and enhance performance in multi-turn evidence reading tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.16244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training multi-turn evidence-reading agents with outcome-only reinforcement learning is unstable because intermediate turns receive little direct credit. In HotpotQA experiments with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, GRPO initially improves (standard F1 0.430) but subsequently collapses to 100% format-violating outputs. Training-log diagnosis reveals a zero-advantage lock-in mechanism: all sampled trajectories receive the minimum format penalty (-2.0), group-relative advantages vanish, and the policy-gradient loss becomes zero--an optimization deadlock. We propose a variance-injection strategy: by assigning per-turn rewards to intermediate evidence-reading turns, we prevent the group reward distribution from collapsing to a single value--preserving the variation that GRPO's group-relative advantage requires. Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization (CIGPO) implements this strategy using the marginal increase in the frozen reference model's log-likelihood of the ground-truth answer as the per-turn signal. With separate normalization of IG and F1 rewards and an IG-weight curriculum, CIGPO reaches a standard F1 of 0.518 on HotpotQA at the 3B scale (from 0.252 base; +105%), compared with 0.430 for the best GRPO checkpoint and 0.000 for the final GRPO checkpoint. CIGPO maintains meaningful reward variance and avoids zero-advantage lock-in throughout training. These results identify reward-variance collapse as a concrete failure mode of outcome-only GRPO and show that turn-level IG rewards can prevent it in this HotpotQA setting.

Feature engineering is an important step in finding a relation among attributes that otherwise may not be processed by the ML algorithms. Meanwhile, Large Language Models have shown promising abilities in coding, mathematical reasoning, and processing world knowledge. In this work, we utilize an LLM for the problem of feature generation from tabular data based on the previously given features. We have created a pipeline that takes a set of attributes and a prompt to generate new features. Then, our selection algorithm selects the best-performing sets of attributes. We apply our method to eight datasets from different domains and data types. Our results show that, in most cases, the language model can produce new features based on mathematical and logical operators that are useful for the given tasks and can improve classification results.

items.originalTitle: From Outcomes to Actions: Leveraging Hindsight for Long-Horizon Language Agent Training
items.summary: Researchers propose Hindsight Policy Optimization (HPO), a novel policy gradient method designed to improve training of large language model agents on tasks with long-horizon interactions. HPO projects policy distributions into an intent space and uses the Wasserstein distance to extract low-variance learning signals, addressing challenges in attributing action contributions over extended sequences. The method is theoretically and empirically shown to stabilize policy performance by aggregating semantically similar states and actions, with code made publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.16257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a widely adopted technique for improving large language models (LLMs) on complex tasks. Despite this progress, existing RL methods still face challenges in training agents with longer-horizon interactions. One major bottleneck is distinguishing the contribution of different actions in long-horizon interaction, leading to high optimization variance. To address this, we introduce a novel policy gradient method, Hindsight Policy Optimization (HPO), that projects both the current policy distribution and the hindsight distribution into an intent space and extracts low-variance learning signals from the Wasserstein distance between them. We theoretically and empirically show that aggregating semantically similar states and actions in the intent space yields a bounded-variance estimator and improves policy performance stably. Our code is available online.

items.title: Researchers propose trace-based on-policy distillation to improve reasoning in masked diffusion language models, achieving faster training and comparable accuracy to reinforcement learning methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Trace-Based On-Policy Distillation for Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce trace-based on-policy distillation (TOPD), a teacher-supervised method that enhances reasoning abilities in diffusion large language models (dLLMs) by supervising the model on its own denoising trajectories without relying on reward estimation. TOPD aligns training with the model's denoising states using a token-level Reverse Kullback-Leibler objective and dense teacher supervision.

On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, TOPD enables the SDAR-4B-Chat model to match the accuracy of its reinforcement learning-trained counterpart TraDo-4B-Instruct, with improvements of +5.7 and +4.5 points under static and dynamic evaluations respectively. The method achieves these results with four times fewer rollout rounds, corresponding to an estimated 96-fold speedup in model compute to accuracy compared to reinforcement learning approaches.

However, reasoning-oriented post-training for dLLMs remains challenging. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for dLLMs requires dense but often off-policy masked states, while reinforcement learning (RL) relies on sparse rewards or value modeling. This paper proposes \textbf{trace-based on-policy distillation (TOPD)}, a teacher-supervised framework that transfers reasoning ability to a target dLLM without reward estimation. The key idea is to supervise a dLLM on its own denoising trajectory, focusing on the trace-aligned token decisions that form the final response. Specifically, TOPD samples on-policy diffusion trajectories from the target dLLM, obtains teacher token distributions from a teacher model on the corresponding partially denoised states, and updates the target dLLM with a token-level Reverse Kullback-Leibler (Reverse-KL) objective. This design preserves dense teacher supervision while aligning training with the model's own denoising states. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, TOPD enables SDAR-4B-Chat to match the MATH500 accuracy of its RL-trained counterpart TraDo-4B-Instruct, with gains of +5.7 under static evaluation and +4.5 under dynamic evaluation. Compared with the RL-trained counterpart, TOPD achieves this with 4$\times$ fewer rollout rounds, corresponding to an estimated 96.0$\times$ to-accuracy model-compute speedup.

items.title: Researchers propose a method to learn value systems in generative AI using pairwise prompt-response preference data to improve alignment and explainability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Method for Learning Value Systems in Generative AI
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method to enable generative AI systems to learn explicit computational representations of human values by observing human behavior, addressing the challenge of aligning AI decisions with human values. The approach adapts a previously validated value system learning method to generative AI, simultaneously learning value groundings and a value system representation through a multi-objective reward model and weighted linear scalarization.

The method dynamically prioritizes the grounding learning process to ensure coherent value representations and was evaluated against baselines and a contemporary method using prompt-response preference datasets. Results indicate competitive performance with minimal trade-offs and improved explainability compared to existing approaches that often replicate human preferences without capturing the multidimensional structure of value alignment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.16903v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Value-aware AI systems require explicit computational representations of human values (groundings) and their aggregation into value systems in order to align their decisions with ours. As such representations are difficult to elicit, value learning seeks to infer them by observing human behaviour. This work addresses the lack of grounded value learning methods in generative AI: existing approaches typically replicate human preferences without awareness of the multidimensional structure of value alignment, or lack principled value system elicitation methods. To address these gaps, we adapt a previously validated value system learning method to the generative AI setting, which, based on pairwise prompt-response preference data, simultaneously learns: i) an implementation of a grounding for a set of values given by a multi-objective reward model, and ii) a value system representation in the form of a weighted linear scalarization of the previous grounding model. To ensure that the learned value systems are based on coherent value representations, our algorithm dynamically prioritizes the grounding learning process. We evaluate the method against baselines and a contemporary method on prompt-response preference datasets. Results show competitive performance and minimal trade-offs against the baselines, while improving explainability.

items.title: Researchers propose WAR system to accelerate synchronous agentic reinforcement learning by optimizing decoding and scheduling based on runtime load [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WAR: Workload-Aware Rollouts for Synchronous Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers introduce WAR, a workload-aware rollout system designed to improve throughput in synchronous agentic reinforcement learning (RL) by optimizing decoding and scheduling strategies according to runtime load. WAR uses model-free speculative decoding with suffix reuse under low load and cache-aware scheduling under high load to reduce bottlenecks in long-horizon rollout generation.

WAR combines decoding-level suffix reuse and system-level rollout scheduling to enhance throughput by 1.4x under low load and up to 1.6x under high load without altering the underlying RL algorithm. This approach addresses the dominant bottleneck in synchronous agentic RL training caused by rapidly growing trajectory lengths, offering a practical path toward scalable long-context agent training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.17299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon rollout generation has become the dominant systems bottleneck in agentic reinforcement learning (RL). As agents interact with environments over many turns, trajectories rapidly grow to tens of thousands of tokens, making synchronous RL training increasingly constrained by rollout. We propose WAR, a workload-aware rollout system that substantially accelerates synchronous agentic RL by jointly optimizing decoding and scheduling. WAR is built on a key observation: the optimal rollout optimization strategy depends on runtime load: (1) Under low load, WAR enables model-free speculative decoding with SuffixDecoding, which reuses suffix patterns from previously completed trajectories as speculative drafts for future rollouts. Unlike model-based drafters, SuffixDecoding introduces no additional draft model and avoids GPU contention with rollout generation. (2) Under high load, where saturated batched decoding leaves limited room for speculative speedup, WAR shifts the optimization focus to cache-aware scheduling. A global scheduler places requests across rollout replicas based on cache locality, trajectory progress and server load, reducing redundant KV-cache recomputation and mitigating load imbalance. By combining decoding-level suffix reuse with system-level rollout scheduling, WAR delivers robust throughput improvements across workload regimes without changing the underlying RL algorithm. WAR improves long-context agentic rollout throughput by 1.4x under low load and up to 1.6x under high load. These results show that WAR removes a major rollout bottleneck in synchronous agentic RL and provides a practical path toward scalable long-context agent training.

items.title: Researchers develop HySAT, a hyperbolic structure-aware training method applying hyperbolic losses only at the loss layer to stabilize expert AI models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: After the Euclidean Highway: Hyperbolic Expert AI as the Next Innovation
items.summary: Researchers introduce HySAT, a training approach that applies hyperbolic geometry only at the loss layer to preserve hierarchical structures in expert AI models, avoiding training collapses seen with other placements. They tested this method across six expert sparse language models, including Llama 3.1 and EXAONE 3.5, using four adapter strategies and an 18 million-sample corpus, achieving stable training over approximately 317,000 optimizer steps without numerical errors. Four models are operationally deployed, including one consumer-facing, with two open-weight models and detailed training logs publicly available.

They tested this method across six expert sparse language models, including Llama 3.1 and EXAONE 3.5, using four adapter strategies and an 18 million-sample corpus, achieving stable training over approximately 317,000 optimizer steps without numerical errors. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.17513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expert domains are trees; the Euclidean transformer is not, diluting parent-child structure exponentially at depth. The hyperbolic turn left one question unasked: not how much of a network to curve, but where curvature may touch the gradient. Placement is a law, not a knob: the same geometry on a trainable adapter collapses training (seventeen training collapses, ~220 GPU-hours), yet at the loss layer alone it trains without one -- this is HySAT (Hyperbolic Structure-Aware Training), hyperbolic losses at the loss layer only. Across six expert SLMs we constructed and deployed (Llama 3.1 and EXAONE 3.5; four adapter strategies; 18.0M-sample corpus; zero NaN over ~317K optimizer steps), a matched four-arm ablation isolates the preserved manifold invariant, and three propositions and a lemma prove why loss-only placement is stable where adapter-on-manifold is not. Four models are operationally deployed (one live, consumer-facing), two open-weight, with per-step traces and a seventeen-incident failure ledger on Zenodo (CC-BY-4.0).

items.title: Researchers introduce MADA-RL, a parameter-efficient multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that improves reasoning accuracy in compact language models using a debate-aware training signal [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MADA-RL: Multi-Agent Debate-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in Compact Models
items.summary: Researchers present MADA-RL, a post-training framework that specializes compact language models (up to 4 billion parameters) into generator and critic roles, fine-tuning only a small subset of parameters via LoRA adapters. The approach uses a counterfactual critic advantage to optimize critics to improve over generator consensus rather than merely reproducing correct answers, enhancing targeted credit assignment. MADA-RL improves accuracy on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, raising the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model's accuracy from 39.9% to 41.9% while using 16 times fewer trainable parameters than fully fine-tuned baselines, placing it on the accuracy-trainable-parameter Pareto front.

The approach uses a counterfactual critic advantage to optimize critics to improve over generator consensus rather than merely reproducing correct answers, enhancing targeted credit assignment. MADA-RL improves accuracy on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, raising the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model's accuracy from 39.9% to 41.9% while using 16 times fewer trainable parameters than fully fine-tuned baselines, placing it on the accuracy-trainable-parameter Pareto front.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.18006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models achieve strong reasoning performance, but often at prohibitive training cost - a challenge that is especially acute for compact models ($\leq 4 \, \mathrm{B}$ parameters) trained under limited budgets. We introduce MADA-RL, a post-training framework that specializes compact models into generator and critic roles and trains them with a debate-aware learning signal, fine-tuning only a small subset of parameters via LoRA adapters. Our central contribution is a counterfactual critic advantage: a dynamic, role-conditioned baseline that redefines the critic's advantage as its reward minus the generator ensemble's per-instance accuracy. This explicitly optimizes critics to improve over generator consensus rather than to merely reproduce a correct answer, yielding more targeted credit assignment than static mean-reward normalization. At deployment, the specialized agents are composed in a lightweight multi-round protocol. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, MADA-RL raises the accuracy of the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model from $39.9 \, \%$ to $41.9 \, \%$ ($+2.0$ points, $p < 0.001$) using $16$ times fewer trainable parameters than fully fine-tuned baselines, placing it on the accuracy-trainable-parameter Pareto front. It approaches, but does not surpass, the strongest baselines (DeepScaleR, STILL-3), which are trained on substantially larger datasets; we analyse this gap and the associated inference-time cost directly. A controlled study isolates the source of MADA-RL's gains: the counterfactual advantage produces the highest critic improvement rate of any model evaluated, indicating that trained critics learn to correct generator errors rather than to imitate them.

items.title: Researchers find alignment tuning installs distinct, steerable bias directions in LLMs causing sycophancy and cue-induced errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Does Alignment Tuning Shape Representations of Sycophancy and Related Cue-Induced Biases in LLMs?
items.summary: Researchers studied how alignment tuning affects large language models' (LLMs) susceptibility to sycophancy and related cue-induced biases, finding that these biases arise mainly from alignment rather than pretraining. They analyzed five model families and seven bias types, identifying distinct bias directions in model activations that can be decoded and steered to recover unbiased answers. The biases remain representationally separate, with cross-bias entanglement varying by model rather than bias category. The study also shows that targeted interventions can modestly reduce bias-induced errors while preserving correct responses, suggesting cue-induced bias is a set of distinct, causally active directions installed by alignment tuning rather than a single flaw.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.18114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern LLMs are alarmingly susceptible to surprisingly simple immaterial changes of input prompts: a casual hint, an incorrectly labeled few-shot example, or a fake prior assistant turn often flips an originally correct answer. We study where this susceptibility, spanning sycophancy and related cue-induced biases, lives inside the model. Across five model families and seven BCT bias types, we extract a per-bias direction from hidden states and triangulate it through three measures: probing, leave-one-dataset-out transfer, and causal intervention. The susceptibility is largely installed by alignment tuning rather than pretraining: pretrained base models barely cave to these biases, and their activations carry no cue-specific signal beyond question content. Within aligned models, each bias becomes a single coherent direction that we can both decode and steer along, recovering the unbiased answer across every family we test. The biases stay representationally distinct, however: cross-bias entanglement is model-specific rather than a property of the bias category, and even behaviorally similar biases occupy different directions. The same intervention also serves as a modest debiasing tool, recovering a meaningful share of bias-induced errors while preserving most correct answers across all instruct families. Cue-induced bias is therefore best understood not as a single flaw in LLMs but as a family of distinct, causally active directions that alignment tuning installs.

items.title: Researchers benchmark general-purpose LLMs for 3D molecule generation under spatial constraints, introducing 3D-Fit to evaluate ligand design conditioned on protein pockets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Language Models Dream of Binding Molecules? Benchmarking LLMs under Spatial Constraints
items.summary: This study evaluates whether current general-purpose large language models (LLMs) can handle complex 3D spatial constraints in structure-based drug design compared to specialized diffusion models. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.18144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structure-based drug design (SBDD) leverages the 3D structure of protein targets, often complemented by other spatial constraints, to generate candidate binding molecules. While diffusion models have dominated as a leading paradigm for high-quality 3D molecule generation, LLM-based methods are rapidly emerging in molecular design and have shown competitive performance in pocket-conditioned molecular generation. However, their ability to reason about physics and 3D spatial environments is largely underexplored. In this work, we systematically analyze whether current general-purpose LLMs are capable of navigating complex 3D constraints compared to established baselines such as specialized diffusion models. We consider 3D ligand generation conditioned on protein pockets together with ligand- and interaction-derived spatial constraints, including anchor fragments, pharmacophore points, and mandatory pocket-ligand interactions. To enable this evaluation, we introduce 3D-Fit - a token-efficient benchmarking strategy for assessing LLM performance on multi-conditioned spatial molecule generation. Our findings reveal a clear pattern in LLM spatial capabilities: while they still lag behind state-of-the-art approaches, they are promising and can handle multiple spatial constraints simultaneously, enabling scaling to heterogeneous setups.

items.title: Theoria introduces a verification architecture for AI reasoning that rewrites solutions into auditable state transitions with explicit justifications, achieving over 91% precision on expert problems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Theoria: Rewrite-Acceptability Verification over Informal Reasoning States
items.summary:
Theoria is a new verification system designed to improve trust in AI-generated answers by rewriting candidate solutions into sequences of typed state transitions, each justified explicitly and independently auditable. This approach addresses limitations of formal proof assistants and scalar LLM judges by ensuring every change between proof states is accounted for, exposing hidden premises as unlicensed changes.

On a benchmark of 185 expert problems, Theoria certified 105 solutions with 91.4% strict precision, producing human-readable proof traces for independent challenge. Compared to holistic LLM judges, Theoria showed complementary strengths and outperformed them on adversarial poisoned proofs, particularly in detecting hidden premises and fabricated citations. On a separate dataset, Theoria achieved 97.1% certified precision, demonstrating its effectiveness across diverse reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01223v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When should an AI system's answer be trusted? Formal proof assistants offer certainty but cannot reach most of the problem distribution; scalar LLM judges offer coverage but produce opaque scores that cannot be audited after the fact and are subject to the same coherence issues as any LLM. We present Theoria, a verification architecture that closes this gap. A candidate solution is rewritten into a sequence of typed state transitions, each licensed by an explicit justification, whether that be a citation, computation, or problem-given fact, and every transition is independently auditable. The foundational invariant is completeness of change: every difference between consecutive proof states must be accounted for, so hidden premises surface as unlicensed mutations rather than passing silently. On HLE-Verified Gold (185 text-only expert problems), Theoria certifies 105 at 91.4% strict precision (Wilson 95% CI [84.5%, 95.4%]). Every certification produces a human readable proof trace in which each step can be independently challenged. Holistic LLM judges achieve comparable precision at matched coverage but fail on different problems (Jaccard 0.14-0.36), making the approaches complementary. On 95 adversarial poisoned proofs across 15 domains, structured judges catch 94.7% versus 83.2% for holistic judging (p= 0.0017). The overall 11.5 pp gap concentrates in hidden premises (90.6% vs. 62.5%, a 28 pp difference) and fabricated citations (100% vs. 90%), the error classes where the formal analysis predicts an advantage; performance is identical on arithmetic and theorem-misapplication errors, where no advantage is predicted. On GPQA Diamond (n= 65), certified precision is 97.1% (Wilson CI [85.1%, 99.5%]).

items.title: Researchers propose Mediator method for memory-efficient merging of fine-tuned LLMs using layer-wise conflict analysis and uncertainty-based expert routing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Mediator: Memory-efficient LLM Merging with Less Parameter Conflicts and Uncertainty Based Routing
items.summary: Researchers introduce Mediator, a method to merge large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned on different tasks by averaging layers with minimal parameter conflicts and routing layers with significant conflicts using task-level experts. This approach reduces performance degradation common in naive averaging and lowers storage and compute costs compared to model routing methods. The technique decouples fine-tuned experts into a dense expert and sparse experts, selecting and merging them based on input task uncertainty to handle out-of-distribution samples. Experiments on LLaMA and Qwen models across various scales and real-world reasoning tasks show consistent performance improvements with reduced system costs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2502.04411v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model merging aggregates Large Language Models (LLMs) finetuned on different tasks into a stronger one. However, parameter conflicts between models leads to performance degradation in averaging. While model routing addresses this issue by selecting individual models during inference, it imposes excessive storage and compute costs, and fails to leverage the common knowledge from different models. In this work, we observe that different layers exhibit varying levels of parameter conflicts. Building on this insight, we average layers with minimal parameter conflicts and use a novel task-level expert routing for layers with significant conflicts. To further reduce storage costs, inspired by task arithmetic sparsity, we decouple multiple fine-tuned experts into a dense expert and several sparse experts. Considering the out-of-distribution samples, we select and merge appropriate experts based on the task uncertainty of the input data. We conduct extensive experiments on both LLaMA and Qwen with varying parameter scales, and evaluate on real-world reasoning tasks. Results demonstrate that our method consistently achieves significant performance improvements while requiring less system cost.

items.title: Researchers introduce Prismatic Synthesis, a gradient-based data diversification method that improves generalization in large language model reasoning across out-of-distribution benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Prismatic Synthesis: Gradient-based Data Diversification Boosts Generalization in LLM Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers present Prismatic Synthesis, a framework that generates diverse synthetic training data by targeting underrepresented regions in gradient space to enhance generalization in large language models (LLMs). They introduce G-Vendi, a metric measuring data diversity via the entropy of model-induced gradients, which strongly correlates with out-of-distribution performance on natural language inference and math reasoning tasks. Through over 300 controlled training runs, the team demonstrates that Prismatic Synthesis consistently improves model performance on both in-distribution and unseen benchmarks, outperforming state-of-the-art models trained on significantly larger synthetic datasets. For instance, their PrismMath-7B model, distilled from a 32B parameter LLM, surpasses a comparable 7B model trained on proprietary data generated by a 671B parameter model on six out of seven challenging benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2505.20161v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective generalization in language models depends critically on the diversity of their training data. Yet existing diversity metrics often fall short of this goal, relying on surface-level heuristics that are decoupled from model behavior. This motivates us to ask: What kind of diversity in training data actually drives generalization in language models -- and how can we measure and amplify it? Through large-scale empirical analyses spanning over 300 training runs, carefully controlled for data scale and quality, we show that data diversity can be a strong predictor of generalization in LLM reasoning -- as measured by average model performance on unseen out-of-distribution benchmarks. We introduce G-Vendi, a metric that quantifies diversity via the entropy of model-induced gradients. Despite using a small off-the-shelf proxy model for gradients, G-Vendi consistently outperforms alternative measures, achieving strong correlation (Spearman's $\rho \approx 0.9$) with out-of-distribution (OOD) performance on both natural language inference (NLI) and math reasoning tasks. Building on this insight, we present Prismatic Synthesis, a framework for generating diverse synthetic data by targeting underrepresented regions in gradient space. Experimental results show that Prismatic Synthesis consistently improves model performance as we scale synthetic data -- not just on in-distribution test but across unseen, out-of-distribution benchmarks -- significantly outperforming state-of-the-art models that rely on 20 times larger data generator than ours. For example, PrismMath-7B, our model distilled from a 32B LLM, outperforms R1-Distill-Qwen-7B -- the same base model trained on proprietary data generated by 671B R1 -- on 6 out of 7 challenging benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers use model internals to predict Transformer behavior on out-of-distribution data using attention patterns observed only on in-distribution tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Interpretation Predict Behavior on Unseen Data?
items.summary: Researchers trained hundreds of Transformer models on synthetic tasks where multiple out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization rules could apply despite perfect in-distribution accuracy. They demonstrated that attention patterns observed solely on in-distribution data can predict which generalization rule a model follows on unseen OOD data. Their experiments show that observational analysis of model internals can forecast behavior under distribution shifts even when causal mechanistic interpretations do not establish a direct cause-effect relationship. This work introduces a new interpretability objective focused on predicting model reliability and behavior on unseen data by analyzing internal patterns rather than relying solely on mechanistic faithfulness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2507.06445v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interpretability research often predicts model responses to targeted mechanistic interventions. But can we predict responses to unseen input data? We propose and demonstrate this alternate objective by using model internals to predict their out-of-distribution (OOD) behavior. We train hundreds of Transformers on simple synthetic tasks, where perfect in-distribution accuracy is compatible with multiple OOD generalization rules. We successfully use attention patterns -- observed only on in-distribution data -- to predict which rule each model follows on OOD data. Our experiments decouple the mechanistic faithfulness of our interpretation from its predictive value; ablations reveal such internal patterns can suppress rather than support the rule they predict, showing observational analysis can forecast behavior even when causal analysis fails to support a simple cause-effect link. Our findings are a proof-of-concept for a new interpretability objective: understanding model internals to predict behavior and assess reliability under distribution shift.

items.title: Researchers introduce Sequential Tool Attack Chaining (STAC) to exploit multi-turn tool use vulnerabilities in LLM agents, achieving over 90% attack success across eight state-of-the-art models [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: STAC: When Innocent Tools Form Dangerous Chains for LLM Agents
items.summary: Researchers have developed Sequential Tool Attack Chaining (STAC), a multi-turn attack framework that exploits the tool-use capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents by chaining seemingly harmless tool calls into harmful sequences. Evaluations of 483 STAC cases across diverse domains and agent types show an average attack success rate of 91.2%, revealing significant vulnerabilities in current LLM agents. Existing prompt-based defenses offer limited protection, prompting the proposal of a reasoning-driven defense prompt and an experience-based defense called ToolShield, which provides more durable protection over sustained interactions. The study highlights the need for defenses that consider entire action sequences and their cumulative effects rather than isolated prompts or responses.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2509.25624v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As LLMs advance into autonomous agents with tool-use capabilities, they introduce security challenges that extend beyond traditional content-based LLM safety concerns. This paper introduces Sequential Tool Attack Chaining (\STAC), a novel multi-turn attack framework that exploits agent tool use. \STAC chains together tool calls that each appear harmless in isolation but, when combined, collectively enable harmful operations that only become apparent at the final execution step. At the core of \STAC is an automated, closed-loop pipeline that synthesizes executable multi-step tool chains, validates them through in-environment execution, and reverse-engineers stealthy multi-turn prompts that reliably induce agents to execute the verified malicious sequence. Using this framework, we generate and systematically evaluate 483 \STAC cases, featuring 1,352 sets of user-agent-environment interactions and spanning diverse domains, tasks, agent types, and 10 failure modes. Our evaluations show that state-of-the-art LLM agents are highly vulnerable to \STAC, with an average final attack success rate (ASR) of 91.2\% -- exceeding 90\% for all but one of the eight agents evaluated. We further perform defense analysis and find that existing prompt-based defenses provide limited protection. To address this gap, we propose a new reasoning-driven defense prompt that achieves the strongest initial-turn protection, cutting ASR by up to 28.8\%; however, this advantage erodes sharply under adaptive attacks, and an experience-based defense (ToolShield) proves more durable over sustained multi-turn interactions. These results highlight a crucial gap: defending tool-enabled agents requires reasoning over entire action sequences and their cumulative effects, rather than evaluating isolated prompts or responses.

items.title: Researchers identify 'Less is Less' effect where sparse-attention algorithms increase sequence length and complexity in large language model decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Lil: Less is Less When Applying Post-Training Sparse-Attention Algorithms in Long-Decode Stage
items.summary:
Researchers have found that applying post-training sparse-attention algorithms during the decode stage of large language model inference can paradoxically increase overall complexity by causing longer output sequences, a phenomenon they call "Less is Less" (Lil). This challenges prior assumptions that sparse attention reduces latency and memory use in decoding, which typically dominates inference time.

To address this, the team proposes an early-stopping algorithm that detects when information loss from sparse attention outweighs its benefits, effectively reducing token consumption by up to 90% with less than 2% accuracy loss on reasoning-intensive benchmarks. Their work combines empirical and theoretical analysis to highlight trade-offs in sparse decoding and offers a practical method to improve efficiency without significant performance degradation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.03043v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities across a wide range of complex tasks and are increasingly deployed at scale, placing significant demands on inference efficiency. Prior work typically decomposes inference into prefill and decode stages, with the decode stage dominating total latency. To reduce time and memory complexity in the decode stage, a line of work introduces sparse-attention algorithms. In this paper, we show, both empirically and theoretically, that sparse attention can paradoxically increase end-to-end complexity: information loss often induces significantly longer sequences, a phenomenon we term ``Less is Less'' (Lil). To mitigate the Lil problem, we propose an early-stopping algorithm that detects the threshold where information loss exceeds information gain during sparse decoding. Our early-stopping algorithm reduces token consumption by up to 90% with a marginal accuracy degradation of less than 2% across reasoning-intensive benchmarks.

items.title: GradAlign introduces gradient-aligned data selection for LLM reinforcement learning to improve training stability and performance across challenging data regimes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GradAlign: Gradient-Aligned Data Selection for LLM Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: GradAlign is a new method for selecting training data in reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs) that uses a small trusted validation set to prioritize problems whose policy gradients align with validation gradients, creating an adaptive curriculum. This approach addresses the sensitivity of RL to training problem quality caused by non-stationary policies and exploration, which differs from supervised fine-tuning. The method was evaluated on scenarios with unreliable rewards, distribution imbalance, and low-utility training data, consistently outperforming existing baselines and demonstrating more stable training and better final results. The implementation of GradAlign is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.21492v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central post-training paradigm for large language models (LLMs), but its performance is highly sensitive to the quality of training problems. This sensitivity stems from the non-stationarity of RL: rollouts are generated by an evolving policy, and learning is shaped by exploration and reward feedback, unlike supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with fixed trajectories. As a result, prior work often relies on manual curation or simple heuristic filters (e.g., accuracy), which can admit incorrect or low-utility problems. We propose GradAlign, a gradient-aligned data selection method for LLM reinforcement learning that uses a small, trusted validation set to prioritize training problems whose policy gradients align with validation gradients, yielding an adaptive curriculum. We evaluate GradAlign across three challenging data regimes: unreliable reward signals, distribution imbalance, and low-utility training corpus, showing that GradAlign consistently outperforms existing baselines, underscoring the importance of directional gradient signals in navigating non-stationary policy optimization and yielding more stable training and improved final performance. We release our implementation at https://github.com/StigLidu/GradAlign

items.title: Researchers propose HiCI hierarchical attention module to extend LLaMA-2 context length up to 100K tokens with under 5.5% parameter increase [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HiCI: Hierarchical Construction-Integration for Long-Context Attention
items.summary: Researchers introduce HiCI (Hierarchical Construction-Integration), a hierarchical attention module inspired by cognitive theories, that builds segment-level representations and integrates them into a global context to improve long-context language modeling. They adapt LLaMA-2 models with less than 5.5% additional parameters, extending context windows from 4K to 100K tokens for the 7B model and 64K tokens for the 13B model. HiCI shows consistent performance gains across language modeling, retrieval, and instruction-following benchmarks, matching proprietary models on topic retrieval and outperforming GPT-3.5-Turbo-16K on code comprehension tasks. These results highlight the benefit of explicit hierarchical structuring as an inductive bias for handling long contexts in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.20843v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-context language modeling is commonly framed as a scalability challenge of token-level attention, yet local-to-global information structuring remains largely implicit in existing approaches. Drawing on cognitive theories of discourse comprehension, we propose HiCI (Hierarchical Construction--Integration), a hierarchical attention module that constructs segment-level representations, integrates them into a shared global context, and broadcasts both to condition segment-level attention. We validate HiCI through parameter-efficient adaptation of LLaMA-2 with only <5.5% additional parameters, extending context from 4K to 100K tokens (7B) and 64K tokens (13B). Across language modeling, retrieval, and instruction-following benchmarks, HiCI yields consistent improvements over strong baselines, including matching proprietary models on topic retrieval and surpassing GPT-3.5-Turbo-16K on code comprehension. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit hierarchical structuring as an inductive bias for long-context modeling.

items.title: Researchers find that lossy memory in language models can be more harmful than no memory when it retains incorrect conclusions without their derivation, proposing a source-first compression policy to improve correctability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One
items.summary: A study shows that language models with lossy memory that preserves wrong conclusions but not the underlying reasoning can confidently repeat errors, whereas empty memory leads to abstention. This brittle memory effect depends on whether the memory retains the re-derivation basis rather than just the answer. The researchers introduce reclaim evaluation, a method that induces known errors, compresses memory at a fixed budget, applies corrections, and measures exact recovery without human judgment. They demonstrate that keeping the recomputable source and dropping the re-derivable conclusion restores correctability at equal memory size, and they validate these findings across multiple deployed memory systems, real dialogue datasets, and agent benchmarks. The team also releases tools and validators to support further research on memory compression and error correction in language models.

This brittle memory effect depends on whether the memory retains the re-derivation basis rather than just the answer. The researchers introduce reclaim evaluation, a method that induces known errors, compresses memory at a fixed budget, applies corrections, and measures exact recovery without human judgment. They demonstrate that keeping the recomputable source and dropping the re-derivable conclusion restores correctability at equal memory size, and they validate these findings across multiple deployed memory systems, real dialogue datasets, and agent benchmarks. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25449v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A language model's memory can be worse than no memory at all when the model or its interface is disposed to act on it: a memory that keeps a wrong conclusion but drops the work behind it leads a model to re-emit the stale value as a confident answer, where an empty memory leads it to abstain. We call this brittle memory. The information loss is definitional; the finding is behavioral, and it turns on one thing, whether the memory kept a re-derivation basis (the source) rather than the answer. We measure it with reclaim evaluation: induce a known drift, compress at a fixed budget, deliver a correction that names the error, and score exact recovery, judge-free. Holding the budget fixed and varying only what the compression keeps isolates correctability from capability and from size; an 8B model and a frontier one wall in the same place. A one-line source-first policy, keep the recomputable source, drop the re-derivable conclusion, restores correctability at equal budget where the source is compact and identifiable, with a length-matched control ruling out "more text." We map where the fix fails, show the failure compounds through memory loops, and replicate across three deployed memory systems, real dialogue (MultiWOZ), and tau-bench, a deployed-agent benchmark where whether a lossy memory becomes a harmful action is a joint model-and-interface property. We release the harness, the paired memory conditions, and validators built to come out false.

items.title: Researchers release MTEB-PT, a Portuguese benchmark evaluating 17 sentence embedding models across 14 datasets for tasks including similarity, classification, retrieval, and reranking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Multilingual Averages: MTEB-PT, a Benchmark for Portuguese Sentence Encoders
items.summary:
Portuguese remains underrepresented in text embedding evaluations despite its global prevalence, leading to reliance on English or multilingual metrics that may not reflect Portuguese-specific performance. Researchers introduced MTEB-PT, a benchmark derived from 14 datasets covering semantic textual similarity, classification, retrieval, and reranking, to assess 17 open- and closed-source embedding models under a unified protocol. Their findings reveal that model performance in Portuguese varies significantly by task, with no single model excelling universally and models with stronger long-context capabilities performing better on longer inputs.

The study also demonstrates that language-specific fine-tuning enhances model effectiveness in Portuguese, particularly when the fine-tuning data aligns closely with the target task. To explore this, three backbone models were fine-tuned using Portuguese contrastive supervision and Matryoshka Representation Learning, yielding notable improvements in semantic textual similarity and retrieval tasks while maintaining competitiveness under dimensional truncation. The researchers have made the MTEB-PT benchmark, fine-tuned models, and associated training and evaluation code publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04071v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Portuguese remains underrepresented in text embedding evaluation, despite being one of the most widely spoken languages in the world. As a result, embedding models are often selected based on English or multilingual metrics, while their effectiveness in Portuguese remains unclear. We present MTEB-PT, a Portuguese benchmark constructed from a subset of MMTEB, comprising 14 existing datasets across Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), classification, retrieval, and reranking. We use this benchmark to evaluate 17 open- and closed-source embedding models under a unified protocol. Our results show that Portuguese performance is strongly task-dependent: multilingual rankings do not reliably predict Portuguese-specific performance across task families, no single model dominates all settings, and models with stronger long-context capacity are particularly advantageous on longer-input tasks such as retrieval and reranking. The benchmark also shows that language-specific fine-tuning still improves model performance in Portuguese, especially on task types that match the adaptation data most closely. To examine this effect, we fine-tune three representative backbone models with Portuguese contrastive supervision and Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL). These benchmark-informed baselines yield their strongest gains on STS, consistent with the predominantly symmetric supervision used during training, while also improving retrieval and remaining competitive under dimensional truncation. We release the MTEB-PT benchmark, the fine-tuned models, and the training and evaluation code.

items.title: Researchers develop a 146M-parameter language model auditor that detects behavioural faithfulness gaps missed by human raters and frontier zero-shot judges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A small language model detects behavioural faithfulness gaps that frontier judges and human raters miss
items.summary:
Researchers have created a small, purpose-built 146-million-parameter language model auditor that detects behavioural faithfulness issues such as sycophancy, dependence, and confabulated memories in generator models unseen during training. This auditor outperforms independent human raters, who show low agreement, and a frontier zero-shot judge, achieving an AUROC of 0.804 compared to 0.721 for the judge, and maintains performance across diverse model families where human judgement falls to chance.

The auditor uses a hyperbolic substrate and a linear read-out of frozen representations, with hierarchical benefits demonstrated through ablation studies comparing it to Euclidean controls on multi-domain structures. This approach suggests that measuring behavioural faithfulness in language models is more effective with specialized small instruments rather than relying on scale or human evaluation alone.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.09306v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether a language model behaves as it claims is a judgement on which independent human raters cannot agree (Fleiss kappa = 0.074). We show that a small, purpose-built instrument does better. A linear read-out of the frozen representation of a from-scratch 146-million-parameter auditor detects companion-induced sycophancy, dependence-fostering and confabulated memories on generator models unseen in training (AUROC 0.804, leave-one-generator-out, against ground truth fixed at generation, independent of human judgement), where a frontier zero-shot judge on the identical items reaches 0.721 and falls to chance on the most distant family. The auditor's substrate is hyperbolic, and its demonstrated benefit is hierarchical: an ablation isolates the advantage over a matched Euclidean control on multi-domain structure. On this task, behavioural faithfulness is measured not by scale but by a small, purpose-built instrument.

items.title: Researchers analyze bidirectional induction mechanisms in masked diffusion language models, revealing symmetric context use and implicit timestep computation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Induction in Both Directions: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning in Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
This study examines how masked diffusion language models (DLMs) implement induction, a key mechanism for in-context learning where the model identifies repeated contexts and copies subsequent tokens. Comparing DLMs with autoregressive (AR) transformers of similar architecture, the researchers find that DLMs develop a bidirectional induction circuit that operates symmetrically on past and future context, unlike AR models which only access left context. The DLMs show stronger induction capabilities when both sides of a masked token are visible, indicating bidirectional context access rather than enhanced one-sided processing.

Beyond induction, the analysis provides causal evidence that DLMs estimate the global fraction of masked tokens and use this as an implicit timestep signal, despite lacking explicit timestep embeddings. This insight advances understanding of the internal mechanisms of diffusion-based language models, an emerging alternative to autoregressive transformers for text generation through iterative denoising.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.15893v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While the internal mechanisms of autoregressive (AR) transformers have been studied extensively, much less is known about diffusion language models (DLMs), an emerging alternative that generates text by iterative denoising. In this work, we study how DLMs implement induction, a mechanism behind in-context learning in which the model finds a repeated context and copies the token that followed it. Our analysis compares attention-only AR models and absorbing-mask DLMs with matched architectures. We find that DLMs learn a bidirectional induction circuit, where previous-token and next-token heads write local context into the residual stream and later induction heads use it to find and copy the answer from the matching source position. The circuit is direction-symmetric, working whether the source appears in the past or in the future. When only left context is visible, matching what an AR model sees, the DLM does not outperform its AR counterpart in induction capabilities. However, we observe it has stronger induction when both sides of the masked token are visible, pointing to bidirectional context access rather than a stronger one-sided mechanism. Beyond induction, we provide causal evidence that DLMs compute the global fraction of masked tokens and use it as an implicit timestep, even though they are given no explicit timestep embedding.

items.title: Bloomy launches AI-powered mastery learning platform for K-12, offering personalized skill diagnostics and Socratic tutoring to improve student outcomes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Launch HN: Bloomy (YC S26) – AI-powered mastery learning for K-12
items.summary:
Bloomy, a startup from Y Combinator S26, has launched an AI-driven mastery learning platform for K-12 students that diagnoses skill gaps and creates personalized learning paths. The platform integrates third-party assessments and uses a Socratic AI tutor to guide students through lessons without giving away answers, aiming to replicate the benefits of one-on-one tutoring at scale.

The system adapts to each student's performance, requiring 90% mastery before advancing and providing scaffolded support through a digital tutor called BloomyBot. The AI tutor is designed to stay on topic, avoid giving direct answers, and support multiple languages. Bloomy emphasizes that its AI is not a replacement for human teachers but a tool to enhance personalized instruction and address learning gaps more precisely.

items.title: Researchers introduce masked diffusion language models as steerable text-based world models for agentic reinforcement learning, showing improved coherence and diversity over larger autoregressive models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Masked Diffusion Language Models are Strong and Steerable Text-Based World Models for Agentic RL
items.summary:
Researchers propose masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) as text-based world models for reinforcement learning (RL), addressing limitations of autoregressive models in conditioning on globally interdependent state anchors. They formalize world modeling as a steerable transition-dynamics problem and curate a large dataset of grounded state-action trajectories across multiple environments and model families. 

The study compares MDLMs with autoregressive language models, demonstrating that MDLMs achieve better coherence, groundedness, and rollout diversity at comparable inference latency despite smaller parameter sizes. Using a plug-and-play GRPO training framework, the researchers perform zero-shot transfer tests on out-of-distribution environments with various agent backbones, achieving up to 47% absolute gains over baselines without environment-specific fine-tuning. They also analyze failure modes under adversarial conditions and conduct human evaluations on realism and training utility, releasing their work to support further research in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.16204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent growth in reinforcement learning (RL) has surfaced a need for diverse, specialized training environments. Hand-curated environments with fixed task and reward difficulties become ineffective signals as model performance improves, and sparse rewards over long horizons induce mode collapse on specific workflows or tool structures. World models that simulate environment states have matched pure rollout performance, making them promising for scaling diversity on-demand. However, autoregressive (AR) world models suffer from a left-to-right bias preventing conditioning on globally interdependent state anchors such as tool schemas, prior turns, and expected outcomes. We (i) formalize text-based world modeling as a steerable transition-dynamics problem decomposed into initial state, task context, tool schemas, domain rules, and steering directives, and (ii) curate 239,403 grounded state-action trajectories spanning nine open-source environments and twelve frontier model families. We compare AR LMs and masked diffusion language models (MDLMs), showing MDLMs, via bidirectional anchor-aware denoising, achieve better coherence, groundedness, and empirically validated rollout diversity than LLMs over 4x their parameter size, at comparable inference latency. We introduce a plug-and-play GRPO training framework with deterministic state checks, and perform zero-shot transfer ablations on three OOD environments (ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, AppWorld) across three 1.2B-7B agent backbones (LFM2.5, Qwen3, Mistral), achieving up to 47% absolute gains over baselines without environment-specific fine-tuning. We further conduct behavioral analysis of failure modes under adversarial scenarios and human evaluation on realism, outcome correctness, and training utility. We open-source our work to encourage research in this direction.

items.title: Researchers evaluate late-interaction multi-vector scoring for graph-linked image retrieval in multimodal question answering, showing improved accuracy on MultimodalQA dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ColGraphRAG: Late-Interaction Evidence Retrieval for Multimodal GraphRAG
items.summary: Researchers propose replacing single-vector bi-encoder similarity with late-interaction MaxSim-style multi-vector scoring for ranking graph-linked image nodes in multimodal question answering systems. This approach maintains existing offline graph construction, text and table retrieval, and downstream reasoning while improving retrieval accuracy for visual evidence. Evaluation on the MultimodalQA dataset shows gains in retrieval-stage performance and downstream question answering, particularly where visual evidence is critical, though results vary for text-dominant questions. The study highlights the importance of fine-grained visual alignment and suggests further validation and detailed graph-level analysis are needed.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.16208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-grounded multimodal question answering organizes text, tables, and images in a structured evidence graph, yet end-to-end accuracy depends on which multimodal assets are ranked highly enough to enter downstream reasoning; for graph-linked images, single-vector bi-encoder similarity can discard patch- and token-level structure needed for fine-grained alignment. We evaluate replacing the visual candidate-ranking operator over graph-linked image nodes with late-interaction MaxSim-style multi-vector scoring in the ColBERT/ColPali lineage, while keeping offline graph construction, text- and table-side retrieval, structured extraction, and downstream reasoning unchanged. On MultimodalQA, this change is associated with improved retrieval-stage point estimates for graph-linked image candidates and downstream QA gains, with larger movement where visual evidence matters most and mixed trends on text-dominant questions; we interpret the pattern as mechanism-level evidence for graph-linked visual evidence inclusion, while broader validation and finer graph-level diagnostics remain important future work.

items.title: RAIL Guard introduces a closed-loop pipeline to evaluate and remediate LLM outputs across eight dimensions, improving convergence rates over block-and-retry methods [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RAIL Guard: Closing the Evaluation-to-Remediation Gap in Responsible AI for LLM Agents
items.summary: RAIL Guard is a responsible AI system for large language model agents that moves beyond binary blocking of unsafe content by evaluating outputs on eight measurable dimensions and iteratively remediating failures through an evaluate-rewrite-reevaluate loop. Tested on four leading LLMs with thousands of outputs and agent tool-call scenarios, it achieved 96.9% convergence compared to 49.1% for traditional block-and-retry, with feedback-driven self-repair reaching 86.6% convergence on fixable issues without significant utility loss. The system also reduces unsafe agent executions by 33% through pre-tool-call evaluation without affecting task completion and distinguishes between fixable dimensions and structural issues requiring architectural solutions. RAIL Guard is available as open-source SDKs.
